extracted.intended_audience: students and mathematicians learning introductory set theory (undergraduate/IMO training)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook-style summary of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with Choice (ZFC), followed by introductory development of ordinals and cardinals: formal language, axioms, encodings, transfinite induction/recursion, von Neumann hierarchy, and basic cardinal arithmetic. Aimed at learning/teaching these foundational concepts and proving elementary results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal argument (Lemma 89.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set X, it is impossible to construct an injective map ι : P(X) ,→ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume ι exists, invert to get a surjection j : X ↠ P(X), define B = {x | x ∉ j(x)} and note B is not in the image of j. The text includes a motivating picture and an exercise (89.2.2) showing how to invert an injection to a surjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal language of set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The language uses the usual logical operators (∀, ∃, =, ⇒, ∧, ∨, ¬) plus only one non-logical relation: membership ∈.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets are referred to indirectly by formulas: e.g. ∃S : x ∈ S ⇐⇒ ((x = 1) ∨ (x = 2)). Elements of sets are themselves sets (numbers, ordered pairs, functions are encoded as sets). This lets us rephrase existence questions as formula existence questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal sentence: ∀x∀y ((∀a (a ∈ x ⇐⇒ a ∈ y)) ⇒ x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Says two sets with the same elements are equal. This gives uniqueness of constructed sets like the empty set, pairs, unions, power sets, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: EmptySet
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal sentence: ∃a : ∀x ¬(x ∈ a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There exists a set with no elements; by Extensionality it is unique and denoted ∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairing: ∀x∀y∃a ∀z, z ∈ a ⇐⇒ ((z = x) ∨ (z = y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given x and y there exists the set a = {x,y}. By Extensionality this set is unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Union: ∀a∃U ∀x [(x ∈ U) ⇐⇒ (∃y : x ∈ y ∈ a)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a set a of sets, there exists the union U = ⋃a. Uniqueness by Extensionality; used to flatten a set of sets into a set of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PowerSet axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: PowerSet: ∀x∃P ∀y(y ∈ P ⇐⇒ y ⊆ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given x there exists P(x) consisting of all subsets of x; uniqueness by Extensionality. Used to define 2^κ = |P(κ)| in cardinal arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation (Regularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no infinite descending chains x0 ∋ x1 ∋ x2 ∋ ... .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, no set contains itself. Foundation enables induction arguments and picking minimal counterexamples; it is used in proofs like there being no set of all ordinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinity: postulates existence of ω = {0,1,2,...} as a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures the natural numbers exist as a set in the universe; used as the base for many constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schema of (restricted) Comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set X and a formula ϕ(x), there exists Y such that ∀y(y ∈ Y ⇐⇒ y ∈ X ∧ ϕ(y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows forming subsets by filtering an existing set X only — prevents forming 'the set of all sets' and thus avoids Cantor's paradox. The text notes Comprehension abbreviates infinitely many axioms Comprehension_ϕ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement schema
rubrics_metrics.description: For any formula ϕ(x,y) that (provably) defines a function on X (unique y for each x ∈ X), there exists Y = f img(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacement_ϕ abbreviates many axioms. Remark 89.4.3 explains the axiom folds in the hypothesis 'ϕ defines a function' into the axiom itself to avoid decidability issues; Replacement often implies Comprehension (problem 89D†).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice (AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal sentence: ∀Y (∅ ∉ Y ⇒ ∃g : Y → ⋃Y such that ∀y ∈ Y (g(y) ∈ y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Says a choice function selecting one element from each nonempty member of a family Y exists as a set. The text remarks the subtle point is that this function g must itself be a set. AC is equivalent to the Well-Ordering Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering theorem (equivalence to AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Choice, every set can be well-ordered; the well-ordering theorem is equivalent to AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-ordering = strict total order with no infinite descending chains; minimal elements exist, enabling forms of induction. Examples and non-examples illustrate when orders are not well-orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding of ordered pair
rubrics_metrics.description: Define (x,y) := {{x}, {x,y}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encoding ensures (x,y) = (a,b) iff x=a and y=b; enables defining tuples and functions as sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of function in set-theoretic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → Y is a collection of ordered pairs such that (i) if (x,y) ∈ f then x ∈ X and y ∈ Y, and (ii) for every x ∈ X there is a unique y ∈ Y with (x,y) ∈ f (denote y = f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual graph-as-set-of-pairs formalization; Replacement uses such definable functions to form image sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Von Neumann definition of natural numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 0 = ∅, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0,1}, 3 = {0,1,2}, ...; ω is the set of all natural numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encodes naturals as sets; remark notes 0 is considered a natural number in set theory and the author uses ω rather than N for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class vs set / von Neumann universe V
rubrics_metrics.description: A class is defined by a formula ϕ and consists of sets satisfying ϕ; V = {x | x = x} is the class of all sets (proper class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper class = not a set. Theorem 89.7.2: There is no set of all sets (V is a proper class). Notation x ∈ C for class C means x satisfies the defining property but does not imply x is an element of a set C if C is proper class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set x is transitive if whenever z ∈ y ∈ x, then z ∈ x (equivalently every y ∈ x satisfies y ⊆ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the definition of ordinals and for checking properties like rank; examples given (e.g., 7 is transitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ordinal
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordinal is a transitive set which is well-ordered by ∈. The class of all ordinals is denoted On.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinals include 0,1,2,...,ω,ω+1,...; properties: α < β iff α ∈ β, and for any two ordinals α,β exactly one of α<β, α=β, α>β holds. Ordinals represent all order types of well-ordered sets (Theorem 90.3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor and limit ordinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Successor: α+1 = α ∪ {α}. A limit ordinal λ is nonzero and not a successor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 7, ω+3 are successors; ω and ω·2 are limit ordinals. Successor and limit cases appear in transfinite induction and recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no set of all ordinals
rubrics_metrics.description: On is a proper class (not a set); proof by contradiction using Foundation: if On were a set then On ∈ On violates Foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 90.4.2 suggests an alternative proof without Foundation by considering On+1. Consequence: any set of ordinals is bounded (has a supremum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sets of ordinals are bounded (suprema exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊆ On is a set, then there is some ordinal α such that A ⊆ α (A must be bounded); sup A exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that unbounded A would equal On contradicting On being a proper class. Examples: sup(α+1)=α; sup λ = λ for limit λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfinite induction principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P(α) for all ordinals α, show P(0), and that for any β, if P(α) holds for all α<β then P(β) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often implemented via the three cases: zero case, successor case, limit case. This generalizes ordinary induction past ω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfinite recursion principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To define x_α for every ordinal α, define x_0, and for any β define x_β using only x_α for α<β (with special treatment at limit ordinals using earlier x_α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split into zero, successor and limit cases. Enables definitions like ordinal addition, multiplication, and the von Neumann hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal arithmetic (addition, multiplication, exponentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined by transfinite recursion: α+0=α, α+(β+1)=(α+β)+1, α+λ = ⋃_{β<λ}(α+β); similarly for multiplication and exponentiation with appropriate recursion rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit constructions: α+β is order-type of ({0}×α) ∪ ({1}×β) with lexicographic ordering. Ordinal arithmetic is associative but not commutative (examples: 1+ω=ω ≠ ω+1; ω·2 ≠ 2·ω). Exercises verify properties and non-commutativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Von Neumann hierarchy V_α
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined by transfinite recursion: V_0 = ∅, V_{α+1} = P(V_α), V_λ = ⋃_{α<λ} V_α for limit λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each V_α is transitive and V_α ⊆ V_β for α<β. Examples of small V_n are given. Rank(y) defined as smallest α with y ∈ V_{α+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: rank(y) is the smallest ordinal α such that y ∈ V_{α+1}. Equivalently the smallest α with y ⊆ V_α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rank(2)=2 and in general rank(α)=α for ordinals. Theorem 90.7.7 (completeness): every set appears in some V_α, proved by minimal counterexample and Replacement to show ranks of members of x form a bounded set of ordinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinals represent all well-order types (Theorem 90.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If < is a well-ordering on a set X then there exists a unique ordinal α and order-preserving bijection α → X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies treating ordinals as canonical representatives of well-order types; used in many constructions and in defining cardinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of equinumerous and cardinal
rubrics_metrics.description: A ≈ B if there is a bijection between A and B. A cardinal is an ordinal κ such that for no α<κ do we have α ≈ κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite ordinals are cardinals; ω is a cardinal, but ω+1, ω^2 etc. are not. Remark about subtlety: verifying κ is a cardinal references the whole universe V (depends on well-ordering theorem/Choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: The cardinality |X| is the least ordinal κ such that X ≈ κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires well-ordering theorem (Choice) to ensure existence. Proposition 91.2.4 restates familiar Cantor–Bernstein-style properties: bijection ↔ equal cardinality; injective map ↔ ≤ cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aleph numbers (ℵ_α)
rubrics_metrics.description: ℵ_0 = ω; ℵ_{α+1} = (ℵ_α)^+ (successor cardinal); ℵ_λ = ⋃_{α<λ} ℵ_α for limit λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alephs enumerate infinite cardinals: 0<1<2<...<ℵ_0<ℵ_1<.... Lemma 91.3.5: every infinite cardinal is some ℵ_α. Definitions: limit cardinals are ℵ_λ for limit λ (including ℵ_0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinal arithmetic (addition and multiplication definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cardinals κ and μ, κ + μ := |({0}×κ) ∪ ({1}×μ)| and κ · μ := |μ × κ|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ignores order; for infinite cardinals arithmetic behaves differently from ordinal arithmetic. Abuse of notation noted (same symbols used for ordinals and cardinals), and ω^α vs ℵ_α distinctions clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite cardinal arithmetic triviality (Theorem 91.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given cardinals κ and μ, one of which is infinite, κ · μ = κ + μ = max {κ, μ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: each is ≤ max^2 and ≥ max, and by Theorem 91.4.5 κ·κ = κ for infinite κ, so equality follows. Examples: ℵ_0 + ℵ_0 = ℵ_0 and ℵ_0 · ℵ_0 = ℵ_0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinal exponentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: For cardinals κ and λ, κ^λ := |F(λ,κ)| where F(λ,κ) is the set of functions from λ to κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular 2^κ = |P(κ)| > κ (Cantor). Continuum Hypothesis (CH) asks whether 2^{ℵ_0} = ℵ_1; CH is undecidable in ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cofinality and regular cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: For a limit ordinal λ, a map f : α → λ is cofinal if for every β<λ there exists γ with f(γ) ≥ β. cof(λ) is the least α for which a cofinal map α → λ exists. A cardinal κ is regular if cof(κ)=κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: map n ↦ ω^n is cofinal in ω^ω; cof(ℵ_0)=ℵ_0 (regular). The text gives a machine-gun analogy for picturing cofinality (how many 'bullets' are needed to reach arbitrarily high below κ).
